claims.claim: Oceanic currents are driven by tides, winds, and differences in water density; winds drive currents at or near the ocean's surface, while density differences drive slower deep circulation.

Because Earth rotates, long-distance moving objects — including ocean water pushed by winds — are deflected to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern Hemisphere; this deflection is the Coriolis effect, and it curves wind-driven surface water into rotating systems called gyres.

There are five major gyres — the North and South Pacific Subtropical Gyres, the North and South Atlantic Subtropical Gyres, and the Indian Ocean Subtropical Gyre — turning clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and counter-clockwise in the Southern Hemisphere, and they do not occur at the equator, where the Coriolis effect is not present.

Ocean currents affect climate by carrying warm water from the equator toward the poles and cold water back from the poles; the Gulf Stream is a strong, narrow western boundary current of the North Atlantic gyre that warms the east coast of the United States and western Europe.

The global ocean conveyor belt is a constantly moving system of deep-ocean circulation driven by temperature and salinity (thermohaline currents: thermo = temperature, haline = salinity); cold, salty water is dense and sinks, and the deep water eventually returns to the surface through mixing and wind-driven upwelling.

A parcel of water takes about 1,000 years to complete the global conveyor's circuit; the conveyor moves at only a few centimeters per second — far slower than wind-driven or tidal currents at tens to hundreds of centimeters per second — yet moves more than 100 times the flow of the Amazon River.

Upwelling is the rising of deep, cold, nutrient-rich water toward the surface, often where winds push surface water away from a coast; the nutrients fertilize surface waters and support high biological productivity, so good fishing grounds are typically found where upwelling is common. Downwelling is the reverse, in which wind-piled surface water sinks toward the bottom.

The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) is a system of ocean currents that circulates water within the Atlantic, bringing warm water north and cold water south, and it is part of the global conveyor belt system.

Tides are the regular up-and-down rise and fall of sea level, driven by the gravitational pull of the Moon and the Sun; currents are continuous, directed flows of water. Tides can create currents near the shore, but the two are different motions.

The conveyor belt is a vital component of the global ocean nutrient cycle: warm surface waters are depleted of nutrients, which are replenished as the water travels through the deep ocean, and the base of the world's food chain depends on cool, nutrient-rich waters.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Naming of the five major gyres.
positions: NOAA Ocean Service 'What is a gyre?': 'the North and South Pacific Subtropical Gyres, the North and South Atlantic Subtropical Gyres, and the Indian Ocean Subtropical Gyre'.
NOAA Currents Tutorial (Boundary Currents): 'the North Atlantic, South Atlantic, North Pacific, South Pacific, and Indian Ocean gyres'.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Both sources list the same five ocean-basin gyres under different naming conventions ('Subtropical' versus basin names); the lesson states five major gyres and names them consistently with the gyre fact page.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How long the conveyor's circuit takes.
positions: NOAA Currents Tutorial: 'It is estimated that it can take 1,000 years for a parcel of water to complete the journey along the global conveyor belt.'
Some popular accounts quote longer, rounder ranges (about 1,000 to 1,600 years).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the NOAA tutorial's 'about 1,000 years' with an explicit 'about' qualifier and makes no precision claim.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Do gyres occur at the equator?
positions: NOAA Currents Tutorial (Boundary Currents): 'They do not occur at the equator, where the Coriolis effect is not present.'
The gyre fact page names only subtropical gyres, consistent with no equatorial gyre.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson only states rotation directions per hemisphere and never claims equatorial gyres.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The machine-generated draft's framing of ocean circulation as a general 'foundational concept' whose main value is organizing information — the draft contained no scientific content, no figures, and no sources, so it was replaced entirely.
The draft's map-legend analogy ('ocean circulation helps you understand what you are looking at first') — not supported by any source and unrelated to the lesson's physical content.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the machine-generated placeholder lesson entirely: it contained no scientific claims, no figures, and no sources.

Added verified quantities from NOAA: five major gyres; about 1,000-year conveyor circuit; conveyor speed of a few centimeters per second versus tens to hundreds for surface currents; conveyor volume more than 100 times the Amazon River flow.

Enforced scope boundaries: tides, waves, ocean composition, and life belong to ocean-systems; atmosphere-ocean coupling to atmosphere-and-oceans; climate to climate — this lesson references them only.
